meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fan Ch'ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, 'It is to love all men.''?
meta.ogDescription: A real passage from the Analects (Book XII.22), in James Legge’s public-domain translation. Confucius’s actual words: 愛人 — “love people.”

answer.label: Written by Confucius (as translated by James Legge)
answer.authorDates: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher & philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine passage from the Analects, Book XII (“Yen Yuan”), chapter 22. The elegant English wording is James Legge’s translation ↗; Confucius’s own answer was just two characters — “愛人” (ai ren, “love people”).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Analects (Lun Yü), Book XII — “Yen Yuan”, ch. 22
Confucius, replying to his disciple Fan Ch’ih (Fan Chi)
樊遲問仁。子曰：愛人。 (“Fan Chi asked about ren; the Master said: love people.”)
James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861; rev. 1893)

source.excerpt: Fan Ch’ih asked about benevolence. The Master said, “It is to love all men.” He asked about knowledge. The Master said, “It is to know all men.”
trail: The passage is Book XII, chapter 22 of the Analects (“Yen Yuan”) ↗, where Fan Ch’ih asks in turn about benevolence and knowledge.
The exact English — “It is to love all men” — is James Legge’s translation ↗; his “Fan Ch’ih” spelling is the signature of that edition.
In the original Confucius answers in just two characters, 愛人 (ai ren, “love people”) ↗ — the expansive “to love all men” is the Victorian translator’s phrasing.
source.excerptNote: Analects 12.22, Legge’s translation. The saying pairs ren (benevolence) with zhi (knowledge): to love people, and to know them.

source.rightsNote: The English wording is James Legge’s translation, first published in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861) and revised in 1893 — both well before 1931, so this translation is in the public domain in the United States. The underlying Classical Chinese text is millennia old and long public domain.

author.name: Confucius (Kong Qiu)
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher, editor & philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu; also Kongzi, “Master Kong”) was a teacher and thinker of the state of Lu whose ideas on virtue, ritual, and benevolent conduct became the foundation of the Confucian tradition. His teachings survive chiefly in the Analects (Lunyu), a collection of sayings and dialogues compiled by his disciples after his death. Here his disciple Fan Ch’ih asks the meaning of ren — benevolence or humaneness — and Confucius answers with the terse core of his ethics: ai ren, love people.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote — with one wrinkle
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Confucius is correct: this is a real line from the Analects. The only thing worth flagging is that the memorable English belongs to the translator, not to Confucius.

items.why: Confucius answered in two Classical Chinese characters — 愛人 (ai ren) ↗. The graceful “It is to love all men” is Legge’s 1861/1893 rendering ↗; other translators give “Love others” or “Love people.”

Online the line is usually clipped to a bare “Love all men” aphorism, stripped of the question-and-answer setting with the disciple Fan Ch’ih and its companion line about knowledge (“to know all men”).

misattribution.truthLine: It really is Confucius — Analects 12.22 ↗ — but the polished English is James Legge’s Victorian translation of a two-character reply.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The exchange is one of the most cited definitions of ren (benevolence, humaneness) in the whole Confucian canon. Asked point-blank what the supreme virtue means, Confucius does not offer a doctrine — he offers a verb: love people.

The passage then pairs benevolence with knowledge (“to know all men”) and a piece of practical governance — raise up the upright over the crooked, and even the crooked can be straightened — grounding the ideal of love in the concrete work of judging and leading people well.
